name: Omar Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, check the solar panel readings on my phone, and have breakfast with my wife Clara. Then I go to the community garden where I run the little sensor system that waters the beds. I talk to an AI assistant about forty times a day, honestly, for wiring questions, for recipes, for settling arguments with Clara. I was an electrician for forty-one years, houses and then some factory maintenance, until my back said stop at sixty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the biggest change in your trade over forty years, and how did you handle it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I loved the moment when the lights come on in a house I wired. I started with a toolbox and ended up reading wiring standards on a tablet. The money was never big. We paid off our little house in the hills last year, and I put solar panels on the roof myself, so the electricity bill is almost nothing. That's what keeps us afloat, because the pensions are small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's useful, just not magic. In my coffee group, the lads who never touched it say it's rubbish and I say well, try it. I use it daily and it saves me an hour here and there. I'd say the sensible thing is to use it like any other tool, a good one but not the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same. The assistant helps me plan the garden watering and check a tricky bit of wiring for neighbours. Money-wise, the house is paid off and the panels cut our bills to maybe 20 a month. So I'm in decent shape, even though the pensions are thin. If prices rise, I'm cushioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do. I'd keep the garden project going, maybe expand it to the school next door. I'd keep helping the neighbours for free with a socket or a fuse box, and maybe teach Clara more of the tablet. And I'd put whatever I save on the energy side into the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, calm. I know it sounds smug, but I've done the preparation. The only thing that nags me is my back, and what happens if one of us gets seriously ill. I don't think about the machines much when I think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the house and solar panels cushion you. How thin is the cushion if something big breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The danger for us is the pension not keeping up. It's about 1,350 for me and 800 for Clara. If inflation goes up a lot, we'd feel it. We could rent out the top room, though. We've got one empty since our son Rui moved to the coast. I'd do that before I'd cut anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the assistant once gave you a wrong wire size. What do you do now to check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like using it, honestly. The assistant is like having a patient apprentice who's read every manual. I know people say it makes mistakes, and it does, so I check it. Once it told me to use a wire gauge that wasn't right for the load, and I'd never have done it, because I know the trade.

say: I'd say use it like any other **tool**, a good one but not the boss.
I'd tell sceptics in my coffee group to just **try it**.
think: The house is paid off and solar brings the bill to about **20 a month**.
My real risk is the **pension** not keeping up if inflation climbs.
do: Keep the **garden sensor** project going and maybe expand it to the school.
Keep helping neighbours with a **socket** or fuse box for free.
Rent out the top **room** before cutting anything.
feel: It feels **calm**, because I've done the preparation, apart from my back.
S0.quote: The assistant is like having a patient apprentice who's read every manual.
fieldNote: Secure because of the paid-off house and **solar panels**, not the pension.
Uses AI like an apprentice, and checks its output.
Warm, a bit smug, and honest about the risk of illness.

steps.text: Keep running the community garden sensor system and add the school
Teach Clara more of the tablet and the assistant
Rent out the empty top room if prices climb

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've been waiting for, mostly. Desk work is going to change a lot, and I'd tell my son Rui, a solar installer, that the paperwork side of his job will be gone in a couple of years and he should get ahead of it. I'd say the assistants are amazing and a bit scary at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually quite good. I can use the tools to keep learning, design a better garden system, even write a small guide to home solar for the neighbours. The risk is my pension, if the government's finances get shaken. Also Clara's niece who works in a bank might lose her job, so I'd worry for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a free online course on solar system design and use the assistant to practice. I'd write a simple how-to for the neighbourhood, 'Solar on a budget,' and maybe charge 5 a copy to cover the printing. I'd help Rui set up a customer app with the assistant. And I'd start a Saturday help desk at the library for older folks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, I'll be honest. A bit like when I first saw a digital multimeter. It feels like new toys. But I keep reminding myself that not everyone is as lucky as me, and some of my friends are really scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rui's office staff might be cut. How would you help him in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Rui's company cuts the office staff, he'd take on more paperwork himself, with the assistant. The installers on the roof would be safe for a while, since robots aren't near that yet. But the people who plan and quote, who book the jobs, would go first. He'd have to be clever and do both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a Saturday help desk. What do older people struggle with most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend Walt (a retired plumber) to try it. He said it's not for him. I told him, you don't have to love it, just let it write your letters. If it's wrong, laugh at it, but it'll save you three hours of misery. That's what I'd say to every retiree.

say: I'd tell my son **Rui** that the paperwork side of installing will be gone soon, so get ahead.
I'd say the assistants are **amazing** and a bit scary.
think: For me it's good: I can keep **learning** and design better systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, wow, okay. This is the real thing. Two years is quick, and I'd say we need an emergency meeting with everyone, from the government to the unions to the neighbours. I'd also say, in our road, we should look after each other. We could pool tools, skills, even meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be unsure. I'm doing fine, but the world around me isn't built for this speed. The pension and the banks are my biggest concern. The house is paid off and the panels help, but if the pension stops being paid properly, we'd have little. I'd be wary of what happens to our 800 euros in savings, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down exactly where our money is and what depends on what. I'd ask the bank how our savings are protected. I'd talk to Rui about whether he and his family could live with us if things go wrong. I'd offer more of my wiring help to neighbours, in exchange for food or other help, a sort of barter circle. And I'd keep learning the tools as fast as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on the edge of something huge. I'm interested, I won't lie, but I'm also on edge. I want to be in the middle of it, not watching from the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a barter circle. How would that work on your street?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no waiting. The thinking work goes first, so my old paperwork and the quotes would be automatic. The hands-on side arrives in 2031, so Rui's roof work is safe till then. That gives us maybe five years to see where things land. Not long, but long enough to build a bit of a lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being 'in the middle of it' mean for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Clara not to panic, because we've got a house, we've got power from the sun, we've got a garden. If it all goes sideways, we can eat and keep warm. Most people can't say that. I'd be grateful, and then I'd make sure our neighbours without that aren't left behind.

say: I'd say we need an **emergency meeting** with government, unions and neighbours.
I'd say on our road we should **look after each other**: tools, skills, meals.
think: I'm doing fine, but the **pension** and the banks are my biggest concern.
If the pension isn't paid properly we'd have **little** to fall back on.
do: Write down exactly where our **money** is and what depends on what.
Ask Rui if his family could live with us if things go **wrong**.
Start a **barter circle** on our street, wiring help for food or other help.
feel: It feels like standing on the **edge** of something huge, interested but on edge.
S2.quote: We've got a house, we've got power from the sun, we've got a garden. If it all goes sideways, we can eat and keep warm.
fieldNote: Pension and banks are his real **exposure**, not the robots.
Plans a street barter circle as a community lifeboat.
Wants to be in the middle of the change, not a spectator.

steps.text: Ask the bank how our savings and pension payments are protected
Invite Rui's family to live with us if things go wrong
Start a street barter circle trading wiring help for food
Keep learning new assistant tools as they appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say, is workable. I'd tell people to get on with it: learn the tools, write the rules, set up local help. I'd say to the council, start a community solar and repair centre now. We could train the retired people to teach each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pretty good about this one. I'd be sixty-nine, still healthy I hope, with a paid-off house and an energy system that works. I'd have time to save a bit more, and to help Rui get set up. The only unknown is the pension and the cost of care if either of us gets ill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with a small battery for the house so we can survive an outage, about 2,800, paid over two years. I'd set aside 30 a month. I'd work with the library to start the help desk. I'd help Rui find a way to grow his installing business, like offering maintenance contracts. And I'd keep up with the assistant, the new versions, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like preparing for a long trip. A bit of nerves, a lot of planning. I like that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the battery for, and why that rather than saving the 2,800?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I can use the time. I can pay off the battery, save up a decent pot, and pass on what I know. With two years I'd be scrambling. With five years I'd be ahead, and I could help the neighbours too, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the doctor about Clara's care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd worry about is Clara's health. She's got a bad knee, and if care becomes expensive or services change, we'd feel it. I'd talk to the doctor about what's available and plan ahead. I'd rather deal with that than a robot.

say: I'd tell people to **get on** with it: learn the tools and set up local help.
I'd ask the council to start a **community solar** and repair centre.
think: I feel **good**, with a paid-off house and a working energy system.
The unknown is the **pension** and care costs if either of us gets ill.
do: Buy a small **battery** for about 2,800, paid over two years.
Set aside **30 a month** and start the library help desk.
Help Rui offer **maintenance contracts** to grow his installing business.
feel: It feels like **preparing** for a long trip, a bit of nerves and a lot of planning.
S3.quote: With five years I'd be ahead, and I could help the neighbours too, which matters to me.
fieldNote: Time lets him **invest** and prepare, with Clara's health as his concern.
Plans for resilience: battery, savings, family business.
The care question is more worrying than any robot.

steps.text: Buy a small house battery for about 2,800 over two years
Set aside 30 a month in savings
Help Rui offer maintenance contracts to grow his installing business
Ask the doctor what care is available for Clara's knee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's a gift. I'd tell people to enjoy the time, and to learn something new each year. I'd say let's use the decade to build local things: solar, gardens, repair shops, schools that teach practical skills. I'd say it to anyone, especially the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel calm, to be fair. I'd be seventy-four, and I think we'd be in good shape. The house, the panels, the garden. By then Rui would be in his forties and might be doing well. The world will change a lot but we'd have time to ride it out. The worry would be health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as now, growing the garden project and the help desk. I'd write a little book about what I've learned with the assistants. I'd spend time with the grandchildren and travel a bit with Clara, maybe a trip to the mountains, which we've always put off. And I'd keep 20 a month in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long runway. I'm calm and curious. I'd want to see the thing arrive, like watching a train come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What do you start now that you wouldn't with 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd probably learn to do some bigger projects with the AI, like designing a community micro-grid for the village. I'd have time to get a few neighbours in on it. In two years I'd be too busy surviving to try that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a village micro-grid need to get started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandkids to learn how things work, not just how to ask the machine. Open up a radio, wire a plug, grow a tomato. Then use the assistant. That way you're the boss, not the passenger. I'd say it as a joke at dinner, but I'd mean every word.

say: I'd tell people to **enjoy the time** and learn something new each year.
I'd say use the decade to build **local things**: solar, gardens, repair shops.
think: I'd feel **calm**, with the house, the panels and the garden in good shape.
The worry would be **health**, more than any machine.
do: Grow the **garden project** and the help desk.
Write a little **book** on what I've learned with the assistants.
Take Clara on a **mountain trip** we've always put off.
feel: It feels like a **long runway**, calm and curious.
S4.quote: Open up a radio, wire a plug, grow a tomato. Then use the assistant. That way you're the boss, not the passenger.
fieldNote: The **longest warning** matches his temperament: calm, curious, planning big projects.
Wants his grandchildren to understand things first, then use the assistant.
Puts a trip and a book on the list.

steps.text: Keep growing the garden project and the library help desk
Design a village micro-grid with neighbours using the assistant
Teach my grandchildren to wire a plug and grow tomatoes
Save 20 a month and plan a mountain trip with Clara

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have the least time and the pension is the soft spot. What would help is a pension linked to prices, simple local help for older people who aren't as lucky as me, and free classes. Also, good rules so the firms don't run off with all the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being calm isn't the same as being safe. I'm lucky: the house is paid off and I'm curious. But my friend Walt isn't, and half my street isn't. Retirees aren't one kind of person. Some retirees run the garden, and some are scared of the phone.

headlineQuote: Retirees aren't one kind of person. Some retirees run the garden, and some are scared of the phone.
portrait: Omar is **64**, a retired electrician with a paid-off house, solar panels and a daily AI habit.
He runs a **community garden** and wants to bring older neighbours along.
His calm rests on the house and panels, while the **pension** and care costs are his soft spot.
He moves between **calm** and **uneasy**, and is most unsettled by the two-year warning.
biggestWorry: Two years worries him most, because of **least time** and the pension as the soft spot.
whatWouldHelp: A **price-linked pension**, local help for older people and good rules on the gains.
